items.title: What the Academie recommends instead of 'email'
items.claim: The Academie francaise has recommended a French alternative to 'email'. What is it?
items.reveal:
Quebec coined 'courriel' first; the Academie endorsed it in 2003. Similar recommendations include 'mot-diese' (hashtag) and 'jeu video en nuage' (cloud gaming).

Usage in France varies; 'mail' and 'email' remain common in practice.
items.why: Official terminology and everyday usage often diverge, sometimes lastingly.

items.title: Origin of the term 'franglais'
items.claim: The term 'franglais' was popularised by a 1964 book. Who wrote it?
items.reveal_title: Etiemble's 1964 polemic gave the term wide circulation
items.reveal:
Etiemble argued anglicisms were displacing French vocabulary and weakening the language. The debate continues in different forms; OQLF in Quebec polices anglicisms more strictly than France.

Great numbers of English loans have nonetheless entered French dictionaries since.
items.why: Concerns about language change recur in similar form across generations.

items.title: Languages spoken in France in 1789
items.claim: Abbe Gregoire's 1794 report estimated what proportion of French citizens spoke standard French as a native language at the time of the Revolution?
items.reveal_title: A small minority spoke standard French
items.reveal:
Gregoire's report 'Rapport sur la necessite et les moyens d'aneantir les patois' estimated that only around 3 million of 25 million inhabitants spoke French well; many used Occitan, Breton, Alsatian, Basque or other languages.

Universal primary education in the late 19th century did much of the standardisation.
items.why: Modern national languages are often the product of policy as much as organic spread.
